articles.title: Checking removable felt pads beneath furniture
articles.summary: Furniture felt pads can reduce scuffs on suitable floors, but loose pads can trap grit or leave adhesive residue.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for checking removable felt pads beneath furniture: Locate pads, Check edges, Record wear. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Identify the contact points
paragraphs: Look at accessible chair and table feet while the furniture is stationary. Felt pads are usually attached to the underside where a leg meets the floor.
Different floors and furniture finishes require different protection. A pad that suits one surface may mark another, so consult the furniture and floor-care instructions.

sections.title: Observe without moving heavy items
paragraphs: From a comfortable position, check whether visible pads are curling, missing, contaminated with grit or leaving marks. Do not tip heavy furniture or reach beneath an unstable object.
Record which furniture leg and floor area are affected. A close photograph of an accessible foot can help identify the size and material without guesswork.

sections.title: Plan an appropriate replacement
paragraphs: For a loose or damaged pad, check the manufacturer's advice for suitable materials and cleaning methods before fitting a replacement.
Keep adhesives away from children and pets, and avoid solvent-based improvisations. Persistent floor marks may need advice from the flooring supplier.

articles.title: Recognising wear on removable cushion-cover fasteners
articles.summary: A simple inspection record helps distinguish ordinary wear from a cover that is difficult to close.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for recognising wear on removable cushion-cover fasteners: Zip track, Pull tab, Seam. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Recognise the closure
paragraphs: Cushion covers may use zips, buttons or hook-and-loop strips. Identify the type before assuming a snagged closure needs repair.
Some decorative covers are not intended to be removed. Look for a care label and follow the manufacturer's washing or handling guidance.

sections.title: Inspect gently
paragraphs: With the cushion resting on a stable surface, note visible fraying, missing teeth, loose stitching or a damaged pull tab. Do not force a jammed zip.
Record the affected side and whether the cover is under unusual tension. A photograph may help a repairer match the fastener.

sections.title: Choose a low-risk follow-up
paragraphs: Avoid pulling hard on fabric or using oils and chemicals that could stain upholstery. If the fastener has sharp exposed parts, keep it away from children until addressed.
For valuable or delicate fabric, use a suitable upholstery repair service rather than experimenting with a replacement closure.

articles.title: Inspecting removable table-leg end caps
articles.summary: End caps on lightweight furniture can loosen, exposing edges that may scratch flooring.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for inspecting removable table-leg end caps: Cap edge, Leg end, Floor mark. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Identify the end cap
paragraphs: Some metal or plastic furniture legs have a fitted cap or glide at the end. It may be made from rubber, plastic or another material.
Not every exposed leg end is designed for a detachable cap. Compare visible legs and any product documentation before selecting a part.

sections.title: Look for wear
paragraphs: On stable, lightweight furniture, look for missing caps, splits, wobbling or scuff marks without placing fingers beneath a loaded leg.
If furniture is unstable, stop using it rather than testing its balance. Record the leg location and any visible part markings.

sections.title: Document the next action
paragraphs: Find the manufacturer's replacement part guidance; caps vary by leg shape, internal dimensions and floor type.
Avoid forcing an ill-fitting cap or using makeshift sharp inserts. Check the floor finish separately if scratches have appeared.

articles.title: Recording visible wear on cupboard handles and knobs
articles.summary: Handle condition notes help separate cosmetic changes from loose or sharp fittings.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for recording visible wear on cupboard handles and knobs: Handle, Base, Surface. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Identify the fitting
paragraphs: Cabinet handles and knobs are frequently touched, and their finish can wear differently from surrounding doors. Record the type and location.
Discolouration may be cosmetic, while sharp edges or looseness can affect everyday use. Do not assume a particular cleaning chemical is safe for the finish.

sections.title: Check accessible surfaces
paragraphs: Observe whether the handle is visibly cracked, sharp, or separating from its mounting without dismantling the door.
Photograph the front and the surrounding finish in good light. Do not tug a loose handle to test it, particularly on glass or damaged panels.

sections.title: Arrange proportionate care
paragraphs: Use manufacturer-approved cleaning guidance for the material. Keep abrasive pads and unknown solvents away from plated or painted finishes.
A handle with sharp edges or obvious instability should be repaired or replaced using appropriate parts before normal use resumes.

articles.title: Keeping a visible condition record for a removable lampshade
articles.summary: A shade can show dust, cracks or heat-related marks that deserve attention without requiring electrical work.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for keeping a visible condition record for a removable lampshade: Shade, Frame, Marks. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Identify the shade type
paragraphs: Note whether the shade is fabric, paper, glass or another material, and whether it appears to be part of a manufacturer-specified light fitting.
Some shades are fixed or require electrical access to remove. This guide covers only visual observation and recordkeeping, not lamp dismantling.

sections.title: Observe from a safe position
paragraphs: With the light switched off and cool, look for visible tears, sagging, discolouration or cracks without touching bulbs or wiring.
If you notice scorching, smoke, unusual smell or damaged electrical parts, stop using the fitting and seek qualified assessment rather than investigating internally.

sections.title: Plan suitable care
paragraphs: Check the manufacturer's instructions for shade compatibility, permitted cleaning and any restrictions on lamp types.
Do not substitute an unknown shade or place flammable decorations near a lamp. Keep a record of the model and concern for the supplier or electrician.

articles.title: Checking reusable household storage crates for damage
articles.summary: Routine visual checks can prevent cracked crates from becoming awkward or unreliable storage.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for checking reusable household storage crates for damage: Base, Handles, Stack. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Recognise common designs
paragraphs: Reusable crates may have rigid sides, folding joints, cut-out handles or lids. Their capacity and stacking arrangements vary.
A crate's appearance does not establish its safe load rating. Read any moulded label or manufacturer's guidance before storing heavy items.

sections.title: Inspect the empty crate
paragraphs: On the floor, look for cracks around handles, broken corners, missing clips or distorted folding joints. Keep fingers clear of pinch points.
Avoid climbing on crates or using them as seats or steps. If a damaged crate is carrying items, unload it carefully rather than testing its strength.

sections.title: Organise safe storage
paragraphs: Keep frequently used crates in reachable positions, with heavy contents low and unstable stacks avoided.
Label the contents rather than relying on transparent sides alone. Retire badly damaged containers and follow local recycling instructions for their material.

articles.title: Maintaining removable drawer organisers without damaging furniture
articles.summary: Organisers can make small items easier to find, but poor fit and trapped grit can mark drawers.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for maintaining removable drawer organisers without damaging furniture: Fit, Corners, Contents. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Identify the organiser
paragraphs: A removable tray or divider sits inside a drawer and is distinct from the drawer runner or cabinet structure.
Check whether it is loose, clipped in place or supplied as part of the furniture. Do not force out fixed fittings.

sections.title: Observe fit and cleanliness
paragraphs: When the drawer opens normally, look for trapped debris, sharp broken corners or an organiser that catches the opening.
Remove only lightweight loose trays where the manufacturer's instructions permit. Avoid overfilling, which may prevent the drawer from closing.

sections.title: Keep a simple maintenance note
paragraphs: Match cleaning methods to the organiser material and dry parts as directed before returning paper or sensitive contents.
If the drawer itself sticks or tilts, do not assume the tray is the cause; record the symptom separately for appropriate furniture assessment.

articles.title: Checking indoor plant trays on window sills
articles.summary: A plant tray can catch ordinary watering drips, but overflow may leave moisture on vulnerable surfaces.

visual.alt: Three-item observation checklist for checking indoor plant trays on window sills: Tray rim, Sill, Moisture. It illustrates what to identify and record, not a dismantling or repair procedure.
visual.caption: Record visible condition first; follow product guidance for any further action.

sections.title: Identify the surface and tray
paragraphs: Indoor plant saucers and trays vary in depth and material. A shallow saucer may not contain every spill, especially on a narrow sill.
Check that the container rests securely and does not obstruct window controls or ventilation. Do not place heavy pots where they could fall.

sections.title: Look for visible water marks
paragraphs: From a safe standing position, check for pooled water, staining or swelling around the tray after normal watering.
Do not lean out of windows or climb to reach plants. Note any repeated damp patches rather than assuming the tray is the only cause.

sections.title: Adjust the arrangement safely
paragraphs: Use a suitable stable tray and follow the window-sill finish manufacturer's care instructions; avoid leaving standing water against wood or painted joints.
If damp persists or affects a wall, seek appropriate property advice. Keep trays and plants away from electrical outlets and trailing leads.
